summary:
TerraTrend is a hackathon project for the "Earth System Trend Detective" theme at NASA Space Apps Challenge Dnipro 2026. It helps people investigate how Earth-system variables, such as climate or environmental data, change over time in a chosen region.

The backend is one Python package, `earthtrend`, with a Litestar API and the analytics code side by side. The API covers a data catalog, investigation "cases" (variable, region, time period), a radar view, history, an AI assistant, tasks, export, an audit log, educational content and sessions. The catalog and radar are open to everyone, and the rest needs a token, which you can get as a guest with one call.

You can run it locally with Python 3.12+ or with Docker Compose, which starts the API, PostgreSQL and Redis. The API code is the single source of truth for the frontend: it generates an OpenAPI contract and TypeScript types, and CI fails if they drift. Tests use pytest with an 85% coverage threshold.

PostgreSQL stores users, hashed API keys, audit logs and AI-review records. Redis briefly caches session checks, and logins still work if it goes down. With an OpenRouter key, the assistant uses a real language model. Without one, it falls back to a local template.

It's still a work in progress. Cases, journal, education, tasks and export don't have database storage yet.
details:
What it does. EarthTrend Detective (TerraTrend) is a web tool that lets students, teachers and curious people investigate whether the Earth is really changing in a given place, using a detective story as the frame. You “open a case” by choosing a variable, such as temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, snow, vegetation or air quality, plus a region and a period. The app gathers the evidence: a monthly time series, the seasonal cycle and anomalies, and a trend line with a confidence band. It then gives a plain-language verdict: “significant trend”, “likely”, “suspicious but not proven”, “no trend detected” or “not enough evidence”. A map then shows the “crime scene”: where inside the region the variable rises, where it falls, and where the change is significant.

How it works. The catalog has 55 variables from NASA missions and models: MERRA-2, MODIS Terra/Aqua, AIRS, GPM IMERG, GLDAS, SMAP and GRACE/GRACE-FO, plus GPCP. Each comes with a simple description for beginners. The analytics engine:

  • weights grid cells by area (cos φ) and removes the seasonal cycle
  • estimates trends with OLS (corrected for autocorrelation, via effective sample size and GLSAR) and with Sen’s slope
  • tests significance with Mann-Kendall and seasonal Mann-Kendall, plus bootstrap and jackknife confidence intervals
  • detects change points
  • controls false discoveries on maps with FDR correction
  • estimates how many more years of data a trend would need to become significant, so a “no trend” result still teaches something

Each case also gets an evidence protocol:

  • Witnesses: do independent datasets of the same quantity agree on the rate of change?
  • Alibi: does the trend survive once climate modes such as ENSO are accounted for?
  • Data-quality checks

Key features.

  • Trend Radar scans the planet and ranks the most significant changes, with correction for multiple testing.
  • Story Lens shows which related variables change together and writes a careful explanation that says “consistent with”, not “caused by”. The text is written by an LLM, but every number is checked against the computed facts. If the check fails, a deterministic template writes the text instead, so no invented number ever reaches the user.
  • Smart variable search takes free-text questions in Ukrainian or English, like “is it getting drier?” or “air pollution”. It uses a fine-tuned multilingual sentence-transformer combined with BM25.
  • Demo cases, a glossary, and exports for reproducibility.

Benefits and intended impact. Professional tools like Giovanni are powerful but assume expertise and don’t explain what a result means. EarthTrend Detective turns NASA data into a guided investigation. Students learn about trends, seasonality, autocorrelation and statistical significance on real data. Teachers get ready-made lessons. Communities and the agricultural sector can check long-term changes in soil moisture, temperature, snow and water storage in their own region, including in Ukraine. The guiding principle is scientific honesty: the app shows uncertainty and limitations instead of hiding them.

Tools and technologies.

  • Python 3.12 and a Litestar REST API
  • NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, Numba, Rbeast and ruptures
  • PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy and Alembic; Redis
  • A TypeScript client generated from the OpenAPI contract
  • sentence-transformers, PyTorch and LightGBM for the ML models
  • An LLM via OpenRouter for Story Lens
  • Docker Compose, pytest and Hypothesis for testing, and validation against Giovanni and Monte-Carlo simulations

No special hardware was used.

Creativity. The detective metaphor runs through the whole experience, with witnesses, alibi and verdict. Other original elements are Trend Radar, Story Lens with fact-checked AI text, the “years to significance” estimate, and maps that show opposite trends inside one region.

Factors the team considered.

  • Scientific validity: area weighting, autocorrelation, multiple testing, and checking results against Giovanni.
  • Beginners: simple language plus Simple and Expert modes.
  • Correlation is not causation.
  • Speed: precomputed products give instant answers.
  • Offline robustness: everything still works without the ML models or the LLM.
  • Language: Ukrainian and English.
  • Accessibility and reproducibility.
dataRefs: MERRA-2 Reanalysis (temperature, humidity, wind, aerosols/PM2.5, snowfall, radiation)
GLDAS Noah Land Surface Model (soil moisture, evapotranspiration, runoff, snow water)
MODIS Terra/Aqua (LST, NDVI/EVI, snow cover, LAI/FPAR, GPP, fire, burned area, AOD, clouds)
Aura OMI (NO2, SO2, O3, HCHO, UV index)
SMAP L3 Soil Moisture & Sea Surface Salinity
NSIDC Sea Ice Concentration, NASA Team
MEaSUREs Gridded Sea Surface Height Anomalies (PO.DAAC)
projectRefs: NOAA Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), used for the “alibi” check
NOAA climate indices: SOI, NAO, AMO, IOD (PSL)
IPCC AR6 reference regions (Iturbide et al.)
multilingual-e5-small, the base model for variable search (Hugging Face)
OpenRouter, the LLM gateway for Story Lens text
Claude / Claude Code, the AI coding assistant
openapi-typescript / openapi-fetch, the typed frontend client
